turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. Gary Pell's here whenever you're ready. I did his spirometry out the front, pre-bronchodilator: FEV1 was 1.8 litres, 62 percent predicted, FVC 3.1 litres, ratio 58 percent. Obs while I was at it, sats 95 percent on air, pulse 88, blood pressure 138 over 84.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yep. Sorry, this screen's decided to freeze. Gary, in you come. Take a seat. What's been going on?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): It's the cough, doctor. Every morning, like clockwork. And I'm getting puffed walking to the car. I keep thinking, what if it's something bad?
[SEG0004] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's sat on this for ages. I'm Helen, his wife. I made him come.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Morning cough and short of breath. How long for the cough?
[SEG0006] person_3 (PATIENT): About three months, the proper cough. I've always been a bit throaty but this is—
[SEG0007] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Three months my foot. It's been since before Christmas, so nearer six.
[SEG0008] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't... look, it doesn't feel like six months to me.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say that again? It logged me out mid-sentence.
[SEG0010] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He reckons three months. I've heard that cough since before Christmas. Call it six.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay. Somewhere between about three and six months, and you two don't agree. The breathlessness, is that the same stretch?
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): Nah, that's newer, the last few weeks, on hills and at the shops and carrying groceries. Not when I'm sitting. Is that how emphysema starts? Dad had it.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll get there. Any fever at the moment?
[SEG0014] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He was crook a few weeks back. You tell him, Gary.
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): No fever now. I had a chest infection, about three weeks ago. Phlegm went green, and it's mostly clear again.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Did you get antibiotics?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah, doxycycline. Hundred milligrams, twice a day, for a week. I finished the box. Chemist in town.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Smoking. Be straight with me, how many a day?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): About ten a day. Well, actually, maybe twenty. Some days. I know how that sounds.
[SEG0020] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's a packet of twenty-five. Don't let him tidy it up.
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): It's not every day a full packet. Maybe twenty. I'm trying to cut down, I am.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Since when?
[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): Sixteen. I'm fifty-eight, so you can do the maths. I was a tiler, retired last year, still the odd cash job, dusty work if that matters. Will I end up on oxygen?
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not from what I'm hearing so far. Any blood in the spit? Any chest pain?
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): No blood. And no... wait, what was the second bit?
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Chest pain.
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Wheeze? Waking up at night gasping?
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): Bit of a wheeze in the mornings, yeah. I sleep okay. I'm not waking up gasping for air.
[SEG0030] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He coughs half the night. I'm the one awake.
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): That's the morning cough starting early, love. I'm not short of breath in the bed.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): What puffers are you on? The screen's still catching up, so just tell me.
[SEG0033] person_3 (PATIENT): Blue one, Ventolin. Two puffs when I'm puffed. They wanted four times a day but I don't do that, only when I need it, so not every day. Is that dangerous, missing them?
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): What's the strength on it?
[SEG0035] person_3 (PATIENT): Um, a hundred micrograms, I think. Might be that. The label's rubbed off.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): And I think there was a preventer. Seretide?
[SEG0037] person_3 (PATIENT): Stopped it. In March. Croaky voice, and I couldn't tell it was doing anything, so I just stopped.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): What strength, and how were you told to take it?
[SEG0039] person_3 (PATIENT): The accuhaler, two hundred and fifty. One puff twice a day. That's what was on the script. Hasn't been near my mouth since March.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anyone offer you quit meds? Champix, patches?
[SEG0041] person_3 (PATIENT): Champix, yeah, a script once. I never took it to the chemist, never swallowed one. Didn't want the patches either, so I never used those.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Medicine allergies?
[SEG0043] person_3 (PATIENT): No. None that I know of.
[SEG0044] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Amoxicillin. Years ago, he came out in hives. We were told to steer clear.
[SEG0045] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't buy that. I'd had prawns the same night. I'm not allergic to amoxicillin. I've said it before.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll leave that one as disputed, I'm not guessing. Other illnesses? Blood pressure, heart, diabetes?

[SEG0047] person_3 (PATIENT): Blood pressure's been high for years. I was on perindopril, five milligrams of a morning. I ran out and I haven't taken it for about two months, sorry. No diabetes, no heart attack.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hang on, the dose. Say it again, this window popped up over the notes.
[SEG0049] person_3 (PATIENT): Five milligrams. I nearly said ten then, but no, it was five. Helen used to put it out.
[SEG0050] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Five. Definitely five.
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): So perindopril five milligrams, stopped about two months ago. Any operations?
[SEG0052] person_3 (PATIENT): Appendix, when I was a kid. Nothing since. Does a cough like this turn into cancer often? I need you to be plain.
[SEG0053] person_2 (DOCTOR): Most smokers' coughs aren't cancer, but I can't promise that off a chat. Family, any lung disease?
[SEG0054] person_3 (PATIENT): Dad, emphysema. Mum's brother, lung cancer. He was a miner, though, not just the smokes.
[SEG0055] person_2 (DOCTOR): Weight loss, bowels, waterworks, anything else playing up?
[SEG0056] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Weight's steady, bowels are fine, waterworks are fine. I'm just scared about the lungs.
[SEG0057] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry, poking in. Did the spirometry land on your screen? It often doesn't.
[SEG0058] person_2 (DOCTOR): No, it didn't. Read it again?
[SEG0059] person_1 (NURSE): Pre-bronchodilator. FEV1 1.8 litres, 62 percent predicted. FVC 3.1 litres. Ratio 58 percent. No post-puff blows today.
[SEG0060] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ta. Gary, any old breathing tests or chest films you remember?
[SEG0061] person_3 (PATIENT): Winter before last, at the hospital. They said the chest x-ray was borderline. That's all I got. I never saw the report, so I can't tell you borderline what.

[SEG0062] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, we'll treat that as what you were told, not a number I've seen. Let me have a listen. Big breaths in... Soft wheeze at both bases. No crackles. Expansion's a bit reduced.
[SEG0063] person_3 (PATIENT): Soft wheeze. Is that bad? Will I need oxygen down the track? What if the puffers don't work? Should I stop the little jobs?

[SEG0064] person_2 (DOCTOR): Slow down. I am not putting you on oxygen today. My working impression is smoking-related COPD, but I can't rule out asthma, or just the tail of that chest infection. Those spirometry numbers show obstruction. They don't seal a diagnosis by themselves.
[SEG0065] person_3 (PATIENT): So are you scanning me? I want a scan if there's any chance of a shadow.
[SEG0066] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not today. We might do a CT of the chest if the cough hasn't settled when I see you next. I'll see you back in two weeks either way.
[SEG0067] person_3 (PATIENT): And quitting? If I book something, will someone actually ring me, or do I chase it?

[SEG0068] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll refer you to Quitline. They'll make contact. Keep using the Ventolin, two puffs when you're breathless, not on a rigid four times a day if that's not how you cope. I'm also starting a preventer, tiotropium, Spiriva, one capsule inhaled every morning, and the script will be waiting out the front.
[SEG0069] person_3 (PATIENT): What about the blood pressure tablet? And if I get dizzy, or the phlegm goes green again?

[SEG0070] person_2 (DOCTOR): Don't restart the perindopril on your own. We'll revisit the pressure at that two-week visit. If you cough up blood, get green phlegm back, or you're breathless at rest, don't wait for the fortnight, come sooner or go to emergency. Cut the cigarettes as far as you can manage between now and then, and reception will book the visit.
[SEG0071] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll get him to the chemist for the new one. Not like the Champix.
[SEG0072] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Sorry I was half inside that computer the whole consult.

features: test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.
interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.
hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

Negative history omitted: no other known medication allergies according to the patient ('No. None that I know of'), though amoxicillin was disputed by wife.

Old investigation history was more specific: chest x-ray was in the winter before last at the hospital, and the patient never saw the report, only recalled being told it was 'borderline'.
